prompt: Which statement best describes the fundamental economic problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Resources are limited relative to wants.

options.label: B
options.text: Wants are limited whenever income increases.

options.label: C
options.text: Resources and wants are both fixed at the same level.

options.label: D
options.text: Resources are unlimited but wants are limited.

explanation: Scarcity exists because available resources are insufficient to satisfy all wants. The key relationship is therefore limited resources relative to wants, not simply low income or a temporary shortage of one product.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why does scarcity make choice necessary?

options.label: A
options.text: Every choice increases the total quantity of resources available.

options.label: B
options.text: A resource used for one purpose cannot at the same time satisfy every competing use.

options.label: C
options.text: Governments can remove scarcity by deciding what people should want.

options.label: D
options.text: Consumers always value all alternatives equally.

explanation: Scarcity means there are competing uses for limited resources. Choosing one use prevents those same resources from being used simultaneously for every alternative, so individuals, firms and governments must make choices.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A student has enough time this evening either to revise economics or to attend a sports practice, but not both. What feature of the situation creates the economic choice?

options.label: A
options.text: The two activities must provide identical satisfaction.

options.label: B
options.text: The student must spend money on both activities.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is unable to rank the two activities.

options.label: D
options.text: The available time cannot accommodate both desired activities.

explanation: The scarce resource is time. Because the student wants to undertake more activities than the available time permits, a choice has to be made between competing uses of that time.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A firm has one production team available next week and two customer orders that each require the whole team. What follows directly from scarcity?

options.label: A
options.text: The firm must choose which order receives the team.

options.label: B
options.text: The firm can complete both orders without giving anything up.

options.label: C
options.text: The firm no longer faces an opportunity cost.

options.label: D
options.text: The firm must stop producing permanently.

explanation: The team is a limited resource with competing uses. The firm cannot assign the same team fully to both orders at once, so it must choose how to use the resource.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government has enough funding for either a new clinic or a new flood barrier this year. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Tax collection removes the opportunity cost of public investment.

options.label: B
options.text: Announcing a budget removes the scarcity of public funding.

options.label: C
options.text: Limited funding requires choosing between the desired projects.

options.label: D
options.text: Equal project values remove the need for a choice.

explanation: Governments also face scarcity. A budget limits what can be provided at one time, so competing projects require a choice even though a government may have ways of raising revenue.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: What is opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: The difference between unlimited wants and limited resources.

options.label: B
options.text: The total value of every alternative not chosen.

options.label: C
options.text: The money price paid for the chosen option.

options.label: D
options.text: The value of the best alternative forgone.

explanation: Opportunity cost expresses the real cost of a choice in terms of the best alternative that has to be forgone. It is not necessarily equal to money expenditure and it is not the sum of all rejected options.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Mina can spend Saturday afternoon on one activity. Her ranking is: 1 volunteering, 2 visiting a museum, 3 watching a film. She chooses volunteering. What is the opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: Visiting the museum and watching the film together.

options.label: B
options.text: Watching the film.

options.label: C
options.text: Visiting the museum.

options.label: D
options.text: Volunteering.

explanation: Once volunteering is chosen, the best available alternative not chosen is the museum visit. The third-ranked film is also forgone, but opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone rather than every forgone alternative.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A firm can use a workshop today to repair its delivery vehicles or to make display stands for a trade fair. It chooses the repairs. What is the opportunity cost of this choice?

options.label: A
options.text: The workshop itself.

options.label: B
options.text: The vehicles after they have been repaired.

options.label: C
options.text: All future output of the firm.

options.label: D
options.text: The forgone display stands.

explanation: The workshop has alternative uses. By using it for vehicle repairs, the firm gives up the next-best use of making the display stands, so that forgone output is the opportunity cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A council owns a hall that can be used tonight either for a youth event or for an adult education class. If it chooses the youth event, what is the opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: The council tax collected during the year.

options.label: B
options.text: The original cost of building the hall.

options.label: C
options.text: The forgone adult education class.

options.label: D
options.text: People attending the youth event.

explanation: The relevant opportunity cost is the best alternative current use of the scarce hall. Historical construction cost and unrelated tax revenue do not identify the alternative forgone by tonight's choice.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: If the value of the best alternative forgone rises while the chosen action is unchanged, what happens to the opportunity cost of the chosen action?

options.label: A
options.text: It becomes zero.

options.label: B
options.text: It rises.

options.label: C
options.text: It must remain unchanged.

options.label: D
options.text: It falls.

explanation: Opportunity cost is measured by the value of the best alternative forgone. If that alternative becomes more valuable while the same choice is made, the cost of giving it up increases.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A student chooses to study rather than take a paid shift. The wage offered for the shift falls, and no other alternative becomes more valuable. What happens to the opportunity cost of studying?

options.label: A
options.text: It falls.

options.label: B
options.text: It rises.

options.label: C
options.text: It is unchanged because studying has no price.

options.label: D
options.text: It becomes the cost of tuition.

explanation: If the paid shift remains the best alternative, a lower wage reduces the value of what is forgone. The opportunity cost of studying therefore falls even though the chosen activity itself has not changed.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which question of resource allocation asks about the types and quantities of goods and services to be produced?

options.label: A
options.text: How to produce?

options.label: B
options.text: When to consume?

options.label: C
options.text: For whom to produce?

options.label: D
options.text: What to produce?

explanation: The question “what to produce?” concerns which goods and services are made and in what quantities. It is distinct from the production method and from the distribution of output.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A bakery is deciding whether to mix dough by hand or use an automated mixer. Which basic resource-allocation question is it addressing?

options.label: A
options.text: What to produce?

options.label: B
options.text: How to produce?

options.label: C
options.text: Whether wants are unlimited?

options.label: D
options.text: For whom to produce?

explanation: The bakery has already identified the product. The decision is about the method used to produce it, so it addresses how to produce.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A housing agency must decide which households will receive a limited number of new homes. Which basic resource-allocation question is being addressed?

options.label: A
options.text: For whom to produce?

options.label: B
options.text: What to produce?

options.label: C
options.text: Whether resources are scarce?

options.label: D
options.text: How to produce?

explanation: The homes already exist in limited quantity. Deciding who receives them concerns the distribution of output among people, which is the “for whom to produce?” question.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which set contains the three basic questions of resource allocation?

options.label: A
options.text: What to produce, how to produce, and for whom to produce.

options.label: B
options.text: Why to produce, when to produce, and where to produce.

options.label: C
options.text: What to consume, where to sell, and when to save.

options.label: D
options.text: How much income, how much wealth, and how much saving.

explanation: All economies must decide what goods and services to produce, how scarce resources will be used in production, and for whom the resulting output will be produced.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A small factory switches from producing mainly school desks to producing mainly office desks. Which basic question has changed?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether scarcity exists.

options.label: B
options.text: How to produce.

options.label: C
options.text: For whom to produce.

options.label: D
options.text: What to produce.

explanation: The factory changes the composition of its output, not the method of production or the way output is distributed. This is a change in what to produce.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A farm keeps the same crop but changes from manual harvesting to machine harvesting. Which basic question has changed?

options.label: A
options.text: For whom to produce.

options.label: B
options.text: How to produce.

options.label: C
options.text: What to produce.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether wants are unlimited.

explanation: The output remains the same crop, while the method of production changes. This is therefore a decision about how to produce.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A school has 30 subsidised meal places and changes the rule determining which pupils qualify. Which basic question is most directly affected?

options.label: A
options.text: What to produce.

options.label: B
options.text: For whom to produce.

options.label: C
options.text: How much scarcity exists.

options.label: D
options.text: How to produce.

explanation: Changing eligibility alters who receives the limited service. This concerns the distribution of output and therefore “for whom to produce?”.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which statement about scarcity is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Scarcity can exist even when an economy has a large quantity of resources.

options.label: B
options.text: Scarcity exists only when all available resources are fully employed and no idle labour or buildings remain.

options.label: C
options.text: Scarcity exists only when people have low incomes.

options.label: D
options.text: Scarcity ends whenever production increases.

explanation: Scarcity is a relative problem: resources are limited compared with wants. A society may have many resources and still face scarcity if wants exceed what those resources can satisfy.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Which row correctly identifies a choice faced at each level?

options.label: A
options.text: Individual: set the national budget; firm: choose a household holiday; government: choose a worker’s leisure

options.label: B
options.text: Individual: eliminate all wants; firm: eliminate scarcity; government: make resources unlimited

options.label: C
options.text: Individual: how to spend limited income; firm: which order to prioritise; government: which public project to fund

options.label: D
options.text: Individual: decide the tax system; firm: allocate every public service; government: choose a consumer’s preferred meal

explanation: Scarcity creates choices for all economic agents. Individuals allocate their own limited resources, firms choose among competing uses of business resources, and governments choose among competing public uses of limited resources.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Luca can use one free hour for a run, a music lesson or extra sleep. He chooses the music lesson and ranks the run second. What is his opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: The run.

options.label: B
options.text: The music lesson.

options.label: C
options.text: The run plus the extra sleep.

options.label: D
options.text: The extra sleep.

explanation: The best alternative forgone is the run because Luca ranks it above extra sleep. Opportunity cost is not the sum of every option that is not chosen.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A firm owns a van that can make either a delivery for customer X or a delivery for customer Y at the same time. It chooses X. Which information is needed to identify the opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: The amount customer X paid last year.

options.label: B
options.text: The total number of vans in the country.

options.label: C
options.text: The benefit the forgone delivery to Y would provide.

options.label: D
options.text: The original purchase price of the van.

explanation: The opportunity cost depends on the value of the best alternative use forgone. Here that is the delivery to Y, so its value to the firm is the relevant information.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A government chooses to use a vacant site for a school rather than for its next-best proposed use, a health centre. What is the opportunity cost of the school site?

options.label: A
options.text: Every project the government might ever consider.

options.label: B
options.text: The health centre displaced by construction of the school.

options.label: C
options.text: The money already spent buying the site.

options.label: D
options.text: The number of pupils who attend the school.

explanation: The site is scarce and has alternative uses. Once the school is chosen, the next-best feasible use, the health centre, is forgone and forms the opportunity cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A teenager ranks four uses of £20: a book first, a meal second, a game third and saving fourth. The teenager buys the book. Which option is the opportunity cost?

options.label: A
options.text: Saving the £20.

options.label: B
options.text: The meal, the game and saving combined.

options.label: C
options.text: The game.

options.label: D
options.text: The meal.

explanation: The meal is the highest-ranked alternative that has been forgone. Lower-ranked alternatives are also rejected, but they do not determine the opportunity cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Which sequence best represents the relationship created by the fundamental economic problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Opportunity cost → unlimited wants → no choice

options.label: B
options.text: Scarcity → no choice → zero opportunity cost

options.label: C
options.text: Scarcity → choice → opportunity cost

options.label: D
options.text: Choice → scarcity → unlimited resources

explanation: Limited resources relative to wants create scarcity. Scarcity makes choice unavoidable, and choosing one alternative means giving up the best alternative, creating opportunity cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

prompt: Consider the statements.1 Scarcity arises because wants exceed the resources available to satisfy them.2 Choice is unnecessary when a decision-maker has more than one possible use for a resource.3 Opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone.Which statements are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 and 3 only

options.label: B
options.text: 1 and 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1, 2 and 3

options.label: D
options.text: 2 and 3 only

explanation: Statements 1 and 3 are correct. Competing uses of a limited resource are precisely why choice is necessary, so statement 2 reverses the logic of scarcity and choice.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | 1.1.2 need to make choices at all levels (individuals, firms, governments) | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.4 basic questions of resource allocation | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A workshop has enough material to complete either 40 stools or 10 tables today. It chooses the tables. What is the opportunity cost of this choice?

options.label: A
options.text: 40 stools.

options.label: B
options.text: 10 tables.

options.label: C
options.text: 50 pieces of furniture.

options.label: D
options.text: 30 stools.

explanation: With the stated material constraint, producing the 10 tables means the workshop gives up the alternative output of 40 stools. Those 40 stools are therefore the opportunity cost of the chosen output.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: Why can opportunity cost exist even when no money is paid?

options.label: A
options.text: Opportunity cost arises only from actual cash expenditure, so giving up leisure without paying creates no economic cost.

options.label: B
options.text: A free activity cannot use scarce resources.

options.label: C
options.text: An alternative has value only if it has a market price.

options.label: D
options.text: Valuable uses of time or other resources are forgone.

explanation: Opportunity cost is about the value of the best alternative forgone, not about whether cash changes hands. Time and other scarce resources can have valuable alternative uses even when an activity has no money price.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

prompt: An economy doubles the quantity of many resources, but wants continue to exceed what can be produced. What has happened to the fundamental economic problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Scarcity has ended because resources increased.

options.label: B
options.text: Opportunity cost must be zero for every decision.

options.label: C
options.text: Choice has ended because more can be produced.

options.label: D
options.text: Resources remain insufficient to satisfy wants.

explanation: An increase in resources can allow more wants to be satisfied, but scarcity remains as long as wants still exceed the resources available. More resources do not automatically remove choice or opportunity cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A school leaver chooses a one-year course rather than a full-time job. The best job available would pay $18 000. The wage on that job then rises to $21 000 while all other alternatives are unchanged. What happens to the opportunity cost of taking the course?

options.label: A
options.text: It falls because education becomes relatively cheaper.

options.label: B
options.text: It is unchanged because course fees have not changed.

options.label: C
options.text: The opportunity cost increases by $3000.

options.label: D
options.text: It becomes equal to the course fee plus every rejected alternative.

explanation: The forgone job is the best alternative. When its value rises from $18 000 to $21 000, the value sacrificed by choosing the course rises by $3 000, so the opportunity cost increases.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A student plans to spend two hours revising. The alternatives are two hours of paid work worth $30, or a sports session the student values at $40. What is the opportunity cost of revising?

options.label: C
options.text: The sports session valued at $40.

options.label: D

explanation: The student cannot do either alternative while revising, but opportunity cost is the best alternative forgone. Because the sports session is valued more highly than the paid work, the sports session is the relevant cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A city can undertake only one of three projects this year. The transport upgrade is ranked first, the library extension second and the park improvement third. If the city chooses the transport upgrade, what is its opportunity cost?

options.label: B
options.text: The library extension.

options.label: C
options.text: The transport upgrade itself.

options.label: D

reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A machine can be used for one day to make either product X or product Y. Making X would contribute $900 toward the firm’s objectives, while making Y would contribute $650. If the firm uses the machine for X, what is the opportunity cost?

options.text: The original purchase price of the machine.

options.text: $900 of contribution from product X.

options.label: D

explanation: Using the machine for X prevents it from being used for Y that day. The value of the best forgone alternative is the $650 contribution from Y, not the value of the chosen output or the machine’s historical cost.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A household has enough money for either a weekend trip or a new appliance. It prefers the trip. Which change would definitely raise the opportunity cost of taking the trip, assuming the appliance remains the best alternative?

options.text: The household values the appliance more highly than before.

options.label: C

options.text: The household values the trip more highly than before.

explanation: The opportunity cost of the trip depends on the value of the best forgone alternative, the appliance. If the appliance becomes more valuable to the household, more is sacrificed by choosing the trip.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.3 nature and definition of opportunity cost, arising from choices | AO2 Analysis

prompt: A country gains access to more resources, but at the same time its population develops additional wants. What can be concluded about scarcity from this information alone?

options.label: B

options.text: Scarcity must have become less severe.

prompt: Which condition would be sufficient for the fundamental economic problem to be absent for a decision-maker at a particular moment?

options.text: Available resources satisfy every current want of that decision-maker.

explanation: Scarcity is absent only if resources are sufficient relative to the wants to be satisfied. Higher income or greater wealth compared with another person does not by itself establish that all wants can be met.
reference: 1.1 Scarcity, choice and opportunity cost | 1.1.1 fundamental economic problem of scarcity | AO1 Knowledge and Understanding

prompt: A ministry changes a school-building plan from 20 small schools to 10 large schools, using the same budget. Which basic resource-allocation question is most directly involved?

prompt: Two students both choose to attend the same free lecture. Student X gives up paid work, while student Y gives up leisure that Y values less than X’s forgone wage. What can be concluded?

prompt: Two councils make the same physical choice to use identical sites as public gardens. Council X gives up a lease opportunity worth $60 000; council Y gives up a lease opportunity worth $15 000. Which conclusion is best?

options.label: A
options.text: Identical sites and uses establish identical opportunity costs.

options.label: B
options.text: Different best forgone alternatives establish different opportunity costs.

options.label: C
options.text: Existing public ownership establishes a zero opportunity cost.

options.label: D
options.text: Identical physical choices establish construction cost as opportunity cost.

explanation: Opportunity cost depends on the value of the best alternative forgone. Even with identical sites and the same chosen use, X sacrifices a $60 000 lease opportunity while Y sacrifices a $15 000 opportunity, so their opportunity costs differ.

prompt: A scholarship pays all tuition for a student who chooses university rather than the best available full-time job. Which statement about the opportunity cost of university is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It equals the scholarship payment because that is the only value connected with the choice.

options.label: B
options.text: It becomes zero because a scholarship removes every economic sacrifice from studying.

options.label: C
options.text: Scarcity disappears because subsidised education does not use limited time or resources.

options.label: D
options.text: It can remain high because the best alternative full-time job is still forgone.

explanation: Removing tuition reduces the money cost of university but does not remove the alternative use of the student’s time. If the full-time job is the best alternative, its value remains an opportunity cost of studying.

prompt: A business owns a building outright. It uses the building for its own office, although another firm would rent it for $40 000 a year. What best illustrates the opportunity cost of using the building as its own office?

options.label: A
options.text: The office revenue earned, because the benefit of the chosen use is its opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: $40 000 of forgone rent, if leasing is the best alternative use.

options.label: C
options.text: Zero, because a building already owned by the firm cannot have an alternative-use cost.

options.label: D
options.text: The original purchase price, because historical expenditure is always the best alternative.

explanation: A resource can have an opportunity cost even when it is already owned. If renting the building is the best alternative use, the $40 000 forgone rent measures the value sacrificed by using it as the firm’s own office.

prompt: A government owns a waterfront site and chooses to use it as a public park. The best feasible alternative is to lease the site for a market. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Every possible future use of the site must be added together to measure opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: The park has no opportunity cost because the government already owns the waterfront site.

options.label: C
options.text: The forgone market lease is relevant if it is the best feasible alternative use.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the cash spent planting and maintaining the park can form its opportunity cost.

explanation: The owned site remains scarce and has an alternative use. Choosing the park means giving up the best feasible alternative, so the value of leasing the site for the market is relevant to the opportunity cost.

prompt: A decision-maker has two equally valued best alternatives to the chosen option. Which statement is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The opportunity cost is zero because a tied ranking means there is no next-best option.

options.label: B
options.text: The opportunity cost is the sum of both alternatives because both are equally preferred.

options.label: C
options.text: Ties prevent identification.

options.label: D
options.text: The opportunity cost is the value of either tied alternative.

explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative forgone. If two feasible alternatives tie for best, either represents the same highest forgone value; adding them would overstate the sacrifice because only one could have been chosen instead.

prompt: A family can choose one of two complete weekend plans. Plan A is chosen. Plan B combines several activities and is the best feasible alternative. What is the opportunity cost of Plan A?

options.label: B
options.text: The value of Plan A plus Plan B.

options.label: C
options.text: The money cost of Plan A.

options.label: D
options.text: Only the single most expensive activity in Plan B.

explanation: The relevant alternative is the complete feasible plan that would have been chosen instead. Because Plan B is the best alternative bundle, its total value is the opportunity cost of choosing Plan A.

prompt: An economy has idle workers and unused buildings, yet many wants remain unsatisfied and some essential resources are limited. Which conclusion is best?

options.text: Idle resources can coexist with scarcity of other essential inputs.

options.label: B
options.text: All opportunity costs must be zero until every resource is used.

options.label: C
options.text: Scarcity is impossible whenever any resource is idle.

options.label: D
options.text: The economy can necessarily satisfy every want using only the idle resources.

explanation: Scarcity concerns the overall relationship between available resources and wants. Some resources may be idle while other necessary resources remain limited, so unsatisfied wants and competing uses can still create scarcity.

prompt: A shop has more units of one product than it can sell today. Which statement about scarcity is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: Scarcity has ended because an unsold product proves that all resources are abundant.

options.label: B
options.text: Opportunity cost is zero for every resource used to produce an unsold product.

options.label: C

options.label: D

prompt: Nadia initially has one free hour. She chooses revision; her next-best alternative is paid work worth $20. Later she has two free hours, enough to revise for one hour and also work for one hour. Her best alternative to the hour of revision is now leisure valued at $12. What happens to the opportunity cost of the revision hour?

options.label: A
options.text: It becomes zero because she can now both revise and work.

options.label: B
options.text: It remains $20 because paid work was originally second best.

options.label: C
options.text: It rises because Nadia has more time.

options.label: D
options.text: It falls from the value of the paid work to the value of leisure.

explanation: With the original one-hour constraint, revision displaced the $20 work shift. Once Nadia has enough time to do both revision and work, paid work is no longer forgone; leisure at $12 becomes the best alternative use of the revision hour, so opportunity cost falls.

prompt: A government can use a budget increase to fund project X without cancelling project Y, which was previously the best alternative to X. However, funding X now requires giving up project Z, valued less than Y. What happens to the opportunity cost of X?

options.label: A
options.text: It becomes Y plus Z because every project not selected must be counted in opportunity cost.

options.label: B
options.text: It falls because Z, not Y, is now the best alternative actually forgone.

options.label: C
options.text: It stays equal to Y because the original second-best project fixes opportunity cost permanently.

options.label: D
options.text: It rises because any increase in the budget necessarily increases the value of what is forgone.

explanation: Opportunity cost is determined by the best alternative that is actually forgone under the current constraint. Once Y can also be funded, it is no longer sacrificed; the lower-valued Z becomes the relevant alternative, so the opportunity cost of X falls.

prompt: A firm says, “We have no opportunity cost because we chose the project with the highest expected benefit.” Which response is best?

options.label: A
options.text: The statement is wrong only when the chosen project requires an explicit cash payment.

options.label: B
options.text: The statement is correct whenever the chosen project earns a positive financial return.

options.label: C
options.text: The statement is wrong because the next-best feasible project is still forgone.

options.label: D
options.text: The statement is correct because opportunity cost exists only when the chosen project is inferior.

explanation: Choosing the highest-valued option does not make the forgone alternatives disappear. The next-best feasible option still has value, and giving it up is the opportunity cost of the chosen project.

prompt: A minister argues, “If we print enough money, the government will no longer face scarcity.” Which response best applies the economic problem?

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is correct because governments, unlike firms and households, do not face choices.

options.text: Money can increase without making the real resources needed for all wants unlimited.

options.label: D

explanation: Scarcity concerns real resources relative to wants. Increasing the amount of money does not automatically increase the real labour, land, equipment, time and other resources required for every desired use, so choices remain necessary.
